Gold for Life

By: Kate Barry | Commission

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
A whistle blower has come forward to give details of how customers are scammed by Gold for Life. According to him "They are selling coins they don't have."
They might have coins in their Scoin shops in various malls throughout the country, but these are purely for display purposes. Even if you pay cash for a coin, or set of coins, they will not hand it over straightaway.
They have a mandatory 45 working days collection policy. After the 45 days has passed, that's when the real wait begins. They will come up with a multitude of excuses and hoops to jump through before you can collect your coins.
Another scam is the safe custody option, SafeGold, where they offer to store your gold coins for a fee: 1 year - R1500; 3 year - R3500; 5 year - R5500; 10 years - R10 000. This includes insurance in the event that your coins are stolen. If you want to collect your coins you have to provide a POP to show you are paid up for this service. You also sign a contract with clear terms and conditions. However, our whistleblower claims there is NO safe custody. They simply sell your coins and when you notify them of your intention to collect, they will make you wait months, if not years before you get your coins.

Summary:
Following on our previous story which showed how the Scoin shops "collectible" Mandela coins are not a worthwhile investment, we will show how Gold for Life (a subsidiary of Scoin and the SA Gold Exchange - all owned by Alan Demby & son Rael Demby) targets low income South Africans with the promise of a safe investment. However, their products are over-priced, and once the sale is concluded customers have to wait months of not years to receive their coins.
What's more they are paying for safe storage of their coins, when in fact there is no vault or storage facility. This amounts to fraud.

Further information:
The Scoin shop's Mandela coins are minted in Norway because the SA Mint refused to make them here. Most customers who pay a premium for these coins, are then offered less than half their value when they want to sell them.
One case study has been notified that he can collect his coins on Friday 7 March from Head Office at The Marc.
Gold for Life, Scoin and the SA Gold Exchange are NOT members of SAAND.
SAAND (South African Association of Numismatic Dealers) is a respected organization with reputable and trustworthy members in the numismatic industry. Our members aim to promote fairness and transparency in the buying and selling of rare and collectible coins.

GOLD FOR LIFE - DRAFT 3

V/O: A weekend funeral in the Free State. The woman being laid to rest here today is the daughter of a single mother who bought into a dream – gold Mandela coins.

V/O: Patricia Ramphene passed away in 2022. Her daughter Refiloe tried to collect those coins from safe custody last year, but the claim is still unresolved. And now she too is going to her grave - without ever seeing her inheritance.

It’s a real fear held by many other customers of the company that sold Patricia the coins: Gold for Life.
01:04:17
Hantise: They know I’m just about to go to the grave. So, if I die, the chapter can be closed down.

V/O: Gold For Life claims to have no record of Refiloe’s request. But dozens of other clients have voiced their concerns.

V/O: So, did this company fool customers who thought they were investing wisely?
And did it dupe a leading Scandinavian Mint and the Nelson Mandela Foundation?

Fade to Black

V/O: The man behind the business is Alan Demby. He’s been trading gold coins for decades through the SA Gold Coin Exchange, Gold for Life and Scoin. His son Rael is now the CEO.

Nelson: Gold for Life to me, was something new in 2013.

V/O: 76-year-old Nelson Hantise lives in Kuruman. Blind since the age of 40 he relies on his wife Mary, a retired teacher, to be his eyes. They travelled to Johannesburg to share their story. Between them they spent R167 000 on Mandela coins, but now they fear losing everything.
00:10:28
Nelson: Hard cash was paid over the counter at Standard Bank.

V/O: Proof of payment was faxed to Gold For Life. Once paid in full, they were presented with Certificates of Ownership - a nest egg for their retirement.

Govan: This is your life savings?

Nelson: For sure.

V/O: But now that they need those life savings, they can’t get them. Since May last year the Hantises have struggled to claim their coins. Gold for Life demanded a long list of certified documents and the Hantises jumped through all the hoops. They even kept some original deposit slips.

Link: But they don’t just want those deposit slips, Gold for Life want the Hantises to go to their bank to get proof for 38 months, going back to 2014.

Nelson: I said to them, you do have all those things. Why can’t you go through your documents or your papers.

Govan: What did they say?

Nelson: No, if you can’t give us proof of payments, we cannot continue

V/O: We asked lawyer Ian Levitt about this demand.
00:04:10
Levitt: They should, as an accountable institution have documentation and records for coins that they issued Certificates of Ownership for. Why do they then have to say to somebody please provide proof of deposits for cash 20 years ago. I believe this company started in 1983. Who keeps the cash deposit slips?
00:02:59
Link: So, Gold for Life says they maintain the highest standards of compliance with FICA and anti-money-laundering regulations. And that’s the reason for the delays.
00:21:41
Ian: So why then ask them for an up-to-date information when you were obliged to have the information in the first place?

V/O: But now a whistle-blower has made startling allegations.
00:36:25
Mavuso: It’s a delaying tactic and not wanting to give clients what they have bought, because they don’t have what clients bought.

V/O: Johannes Mavuso is a former Client Service Manager at Gold for Life. In his seven years with the company, he dealt with hundreds of complaints.

Mavuso: They’re making money in selling gold coins that they don’t have. They might be having two or three sets there, but you’re paying over a period of time and you’re not eventually collecting. And when it’s time for them to deliver, you will get a run-around; you can’t be getting what you bought.

Govan: Does Gold for Life deliberately delay people?

Mavuso: Yes, it does, it does.

Govan: Do the people working there know they’re being told to delay clients?

Mavuso: Yes, they know.

V/O: But Gold for Life denies there are undue delays. They’re maintaining rigorous diligence, and it’s identity fraud, non-matching signatures and missing documents delaying delivery.

Text: There are no undue delays. We deal in large numbers … and must maintain rigorous diligence.

Issues such as identity fraud, non-matching signatures and missing original documents delay deliveries.
V/O: But Mary Hantise received this email showing how unreasonable the delays are: a six month wait for forms.
Email Text: You have been added to the waiting list for coin release request. Please be patient there are a high volume of coin release. I can only forward the forms in 2025.
Ian: Why? I mean, it’s obvious to me that they don’t have the coins.
00:23:52 We now see a letter like this that says in 2024: don’t call me, we’ll call you in 2025 because there’s such a big backlog of requests for coins. And they don’t say that the reason for having done so is a contractual issue, this is just nonsense!
V/O: This man - who we’ll call Richard – is an IT manager and a father-of-two. In 2010 he bought Mandela coins for R55 000. He later swapped them for Kruger rands and bought two more Kruger Rands sets. He’s still paying off one.
Govan: Once you had paid for your coins where did you keep them?
00:12:41
Richard: They’re saying look, we can keep it for you, very safe, for a small fee; an annual fee.

V/O: Both Richard and the Hantises entrusted their coins to SafeGold, also owned by Alan Demby. SafeGold’s marketing brochure suggests a vault. But Mavuso says the picture is a fiction.

Steven: SafeGold, it’s just a word on a wall. There is no SafeGold where you can take a key and open, then see your coins are being stored and kept. There is no such. They’re selling you the idea of SafeGold. There’s no SafeGold.

V/O: Demby says this allegation is incorrect. They maintain secure, insured vaults, not to be disclosed for security reasons.

Text: This allegation is blatantly uncorroborated and incorrect. We maintain secure, insured vaults for safekeeping, not to be disclosed for obvious security reasons.

V/O: In May last year Richard wanted to collect his Kruger rands. He got the standard response: Expect a delay.

Text: You have been added to the coin release list, expect a delay due to high volume requests.

V/O: By July he’d jumped through all the FICA hoops, but was then told to wait until September.
00:28:20
Richard: I said Hey! 45 days has arrived. Can I come to your office tomorrow?
00:29:00
Govan: What was the reply?
00:29:14
Richard: We are waiting for management approval. Then, eventually, after a month, management has approved. Oh finally, yes! Can I come and collect? No. We are going on stock take.

Govan: Stock take?


Richard: Give us a week or so.
Now they’re ignoring me. No one is responding to me, and I’m getting agitated. Six months. Why are they sending me from pillar to post to collect my own items?

V/O: Eventually his lawyer sent Gold for Life a letter of demand.

Govan: Did they respond?

Richard: Nope.
00:40:24 It did not help.

Govan: Why was Richard delayed for ten months?

Mavuso: I think it’s because they didn’t have his coins.

Govan: And is that common?

Mavuso: It’s happening now as we speak.

Govan: When you were at Gold for Life and you had a client who was asking for their coins, where would you buy it from?
01:12:41
Mavuso: I go into the system; I’m checking on that list of clients who collected. I phone them. We are currently buying. Here is an offer.
01:13:19
Govan: It's the same coins that you perpetually put in rotation.
01:13:23
Mavuso: Same coins, same coins.

Link: Gold for Life say the allegation that they need to source coins is entirely untrue. The 45-working-day waiting period is to validate the contract and confirm the client’s identity.

V/O: After ten months Richard finally got a call.

Richard: Your coins are ready for collection. Are you kidding me? When? Immediately.
Sfx: So just to confirm, this is what you’re collecting: it’s the two Kruger 4-coins VIP sets.
So, you can fake the weight, the colour, the size, everything; but you can’t fake the sound. Ping!

V/O: Gold For Life now claims Richard’s delay was because he was in arrears on the third Krugerrands set he’s still paying off.

Text: Delays stemmed from R39,651 arrears. His non-compliance caused the delay – not our audit.

V/O: Demby told Carte Blanche the real reason they won’t release the Hantise’s coins is unpaid storage fees.

Text: Our request for proof of payment relates to verification for release —triggered by unpaid SafeGold fees

V/O: That, and what he bizarrely claims are Hantise’s inconsistent signatures.
But Hantise is blind and signing from memory. This is his e-signature signed with his finger on a phone screen.

Govan: Where are his coins?

Mavuso No-one knows, because there is no physical coins waiting on the shelves somewhere for Hantise. It’s only on paper that he bought.

V/O: Mavuso then made a staggering claim – Gold for Life has sold far more Mandela Long Walk to Freedom coins on paper than were originally minted.

Mavuso: We have sold more than 5000 pieces.
01:17:58
Govan: You’re sure about that?

Mavuso: Yes, correctly so!

V/O: Demby says Mavuso had no access to or knowledge of their inventories or audits.

Text: This allegation is demonstrably false.
Mavuso did not have any access to or knowledge of our inventories or audits, rendering his claims baseless.

V/O: And neither would it seem did the Mint of Norway who originally produced the coins. The CEO had never heard this allegation.

Text: We have no indications to believe that the SA Gold Coin Exchange has sold more medals than what we have struck.

V/O: And her answer was vague, when asked how many Mandela coins were minted.

Text: Each Nelson Mandela medal produced by the Mint of Norway is strictly limited to a specific mintage.

V/O: We then asked the Nelson Mandela Foundation, who gave permission for the use of Madiba’s image. The new CEO is Dr Mbongiseni Buthelezi.
00:01:03
Buthelezi: 1.5% was the royalty agreed upon, based on the number of coins minted.

Govan: How many coins were minted?

Buthelezi: We don’t have the exact numbers.

Govan: Can you tell us how much the Foundation has received in royalties?

Buthelezi: I think the last payment we got in 2022 was in the region of about R20 000, I think.

V/O: In a bid to discredit the whistle-blower Gold for Life launched a social media attack on Mavuso last week. It claimed his employment was terminated because of fraudulent activities while refusing to produce any evidence.
00:48:01
Govan: Did you get fired from Gold for Life?

Mavuso: I actually resigned.

Govan: Why?

Mavuso: I felt I wasn’t actually doing our people right. And I was part of this kind of a scam.

V/O: He produced an email outlining the Terms and Conditions of his Resignation.

Text: Your notice of immediate resignation received via email on 08 April 2024 at 09h37 is noted.
01:06:47
Govan: Won’t Gold for Life say that you’re just a disgruntled employee?
01:06:54
Mavuso: They can say whatever they want about me, but I have resigned. Why I’m hiding my identity? I don’t want people to be coming after me, because I put my face out there selling them this idea.

V/O: The Mint of Norway has now requested a full audit of all the Mandela coins bought and sold.

Text: The SA Gold Coin Exchange has assured us that a reputable external audit firm will conduct an independent audit.

V/O: And hopefully they’re not paper coins. Because with the price of gold shooting through the roof, clients will be keen to cash in.

The woman being laid to rest here today is the daughter of a single mother who bought into a dream – gold Mandela coins. V/O: Patricia Ramphene passed away in 2022. Her daughter Refiloe tried to collect those coins from safe custody last year, but the claim is still unresolved. And now she too is going to her grave - without ever seeing her inheritance. It’s a real fear held by many other customers of the company that sold Patricia the coins: Gold for Life. 01:04:17 Hantise: They know I’m just about to go to the grave. So, if I die, the chapter can be closed down. V/O: Gold For Life claims to have no record of Refiloe’s request. But dozens of other clients have voiced their concerns. V/O: So, did this company fool customers who thought they were investing wisely? And did it dupe a leading Scandinavian Mint and the Nelson Mandela Foundation? Fade to Black V/O: The man behind the business is Alan Demby. He’s been trading gold coins for decades through the SA Gold Coin Exchange, Gold for Life and Scoin. His son Rael is now the CEO. Nelson: Gold for Life to me, was something new in 2013. V/O: 76-year-old Nelson Hantise lives in Kuruman. Blind since the age of 40 he relies on his wife Mary, a retired teacher, to be his eyes. They travelled to Johannesburg to share their story. Between them they spent R167 000 on Mandela coins, but now they fear losing everything. 00:10:28 Nelson: Hard cash was paid over the counter at Standard Bank. V/O: Proof of payment was faxed to Gold For Life. Once paid in full, they were presented with Certificates of Ownership - a nest egg for their retirement. Govan: This is your life savings? Nelson: For sure. V/O: But now that they need those life savings, they can’t get them. Since May last year the Hantises have struggled to claim their coins. Gold for Life demanded a long list of certified documents and the Hantises jumped through all the hoops. They even kept some original deposit slips. Link: But they don’t just want those deposit slips, Gold for Life want the Hantises to go to their bank to get proof for 38 months, going back to 2014. Nelson: I said to them, you do have all those things. Why can’t you go through your documents or your papers. Govan: What did they say? Nelson: No, if you can’t give us proof of payments, we cannot continue V/O: We asked lawyer Ian Levitt about this demand. 00:04:10 Levitt: They should, as an accountable institution have documentation and records for coins that they issued Certificates of Ownership for. Why do they then have to say to somebody please provide proof of deposits for cash 20 years ago. I believe this company started in 1983. Who keeps the cash deposit slips? 00:02:59 Link: So, Gold for Life says they maintain the highest standards of compliance with FICA and anti-money-laundering regulations. And that’s the reason for the delays. 00:21:41 Ian: So why then ask them for an up-to-date information when you were obliged to have the information in the first place? V/O: But now a whistle-blower has made startling allegations. 00:36:25 Mavuso: It’s a delaying tactic and not wanting to give clients what they have bought, because they don’t have what clients bought. V/O: Johannes Mavuso is a former Client Service Manager at Gold for Life. In his seven years with the company, he dealt with hundreds of complaints. Mavuso: They’re making money in selling gold coins that they don’t have. They might be having two or three sets there, but you’re paying over a period of time and you’re not eventually collecting. And when it’s time for them to deliver, you will get a run-around; you can’t be getting what you bought. Govan: Does Gold for Life deliberately delay people? Mavuso: Yes, it does, it does. Govan: Do the people working there know they’re being told to delay clients? Mavuso: Yes, they know. V/O: But Gold for Life denies there are undue delays. They’re maintaining rigorous diligence, and it’s identity fraud, non-matching signatures and missing documents delaying delivery. Text: There are no undue delays. We deal in large numbers … and must maintain rigorous diligence. Issues such as identity fraud, non-matching signatures and missing original documents delay deliveries. V/O: But Mary Hantise received this email showing how unreasonable the delays are: a six month wait for forms. Email Text: You have been added to the waiting list for coin release request. Please be patient there are a high volume of coin release. I can only forward the forms in 2025. Ian: Why? I mean, it’s obvious to me that they don’t have the coins. 00:23:52 We now see a letter like this that says in 2024: don’t call me, we’ll call you in 2025 because there’s such a big backlog of requests for coins. And they don’t say that the reason for having done so is a contractual issue, this is just nonsense! V/O: This man - who we’ll call Richard – is an IT manager and a father-of-two. In 2010 he bought Mandela coins for R55 000. He later swapped them for Kruger rands and bought two more Kruger Rands sets. He’s still paying off one. Govan: Once you had paid for your coins where did you keep them? 00:12:41 Richard: They’re saying look, we can keep it for you, very safe, for a small fee; an annual fee. V/O: Both Richard and the Hantises entrusted their coins to SafeGold, also owned by Alan Demby. SafeGold’s marketing brochure suggests a vault. But Mavuso says the picture is a fiction. Steven: SafeGold, it’s just a word on a wall. There is no SafeGold where you can take a key and open, then see your coins are being stored and kept. There is no such. They’re selling you the idea of SafeGold. There’s no SafeGold. V/O: Demby says this allegation is incorrect. They maintain secure, insured vaults, not to be disclosed for security reasons. Text: This allegation is blatantly uncorroborated and incorrect. We maintain secure, insured vaults for safekeeping, not to be disclosed for obvious security reasons. V/O: In May last year Richard wanted to collect his Kruger rands. He got the standard response: Expect a delay. Text: You have been added to the coin release list, expect a delay due to high volume requests. V/O: By July he’d jumped through all the FICA hoops, but was then told to wait until September. 00:28:20 Richard: I said Hey! 45 days has arrived. Can I come to your office tomorrow? 00:29:00 Govan: What was the reply? 00:29:14 Richard: We are waiting for management approval. Then, eventually, after a month, management has approved. Oh finally, yes! Can I come and collect? No. We are going on stock take. Govan: Stock take? Richard: Give us a week or so. Now they’re ignoring me. No one is responding to me, and I’m getting agitated. Six months. Why are they sending me from pillar to post to collect my own items? V/O: Eventually his lawyer sent Gold for Life a letter of demand. Govan: Did they respond? Richard: Nope. 00:40:24 It did not help. Govan: Why was Richard delayed for ten months? Mavuso: I think it’s because they didn’t have his coins. Govan: And is that common? Mavuso: It’s happening now as we speak. Govan: When you were at Gold for Life and you had a client who was asking for their coins, where would you buy it from? 01:12:41 Mavuso: I go into the system; I’m checking on that list of clients who collected. I phone them. We are currently buying. Here is an offer. 01:13:19 Govan: It's the same coins that you perpetually put in rotation. 01:13:23 Mavuso: Same coins, same coins. Link: Gold for Life say the allegation that they need to source coins is entirely untrue. The 45-working-day waiting period is to validate the contract and confirm the client’s identity. V/O: After ten months Richard finally got a call. Richard: Your coins are ready for collection. Are you kidding me? When? Immediately. Sfx: So just to confirm, this is what you’re collecting: it’s the two Kruger 4-coins VIP sets. So, you can fake the weight, the colour, the size, everything; but you can’t fake the sound. Ping! V/O: Gold For Life now claims Richard’s delay was because he was in arrears on the third Krugerrands set he’s still paying off. Text: Delays stemmed from R39,651 arrears. His non-compliance caused the delay – not our audit. V/O: Demby told Carte Blanche the real reason they won’t release the Hantise’s coins is unpaid storage fees. Text: Our request for proof of payment relates to verification for release —triggered by unpaid SafeGold fees V/O: That, and what he bizarrely claims are Hantise’s inconsistent signatures. But Hantise is blind and signing from memory. This is his e-signature signed with his finger on a phone screen. Govan: Where are his coins? Mavuso No-one knows, because there is no physical coins waiting on the shelves somewhere for Hantise. It’s only on paper that he bought. V/O: Mavuso then made a staggering claim – Gold for Life has sold far more Mandela Long Walk to Freedom coins on paper than were originally minted. Mavuso: We have sold more than 5000 pieces. 01:17:58 Govan: You’re sure about that? Mavuso: Yes, correctly so! V/O: Demby says Mavuso had no access to or knowledge of their inventories or audits. Text: This allegation is demonstrably false. Mavuso did not have any access to or knowledge of our inventories or audits, rendering his claims baseless. V/O: And neither would it seem did the Mint of Norway who originally produced the coins. The CEO had never heard this allegation. Text: We have no indications to believe that the SA Gold Coin Exchange has sold more medals than what we have struck. V/O: And her answer was vague, when asked how many Mandela coins were minted. Text: Each Nelson Mandela medal produced by the Mint of Norway is strictly limited to a specific mintage. V/O: We then asked the Nelson Mandela Foundation, who gave permission for the use of Madiba’s image. The new CEO is Dr Mbongiseni Buthelezi. 00:01:03 Buthelezi: 1.5% was the royalty agreed upon, based on the number of coins minted. Govan: How many coins were minted? Buthelezi: We don’t have the exact numbers. Govan: Can you tell us how much the Foundation has received in royalties? Buthelezi: I think the last payment we got in 2022 was in the region of about R20 000, I think. V/O: In a bid to discredit the whistle-blower Gold for Life launched a social media attack on Mavuso last week. It claimed his employment was terminated because of fraudulent activities while refusing to produce any evidence. 00:48:01 Govan: Did you get fired from Gold for Life? Mavuso: I actually resigned. Govan: Why? Mavuso: I felt I wasn’t actually doing our people right. And I was part of this kind of a scam. V/O: He produced an email outlining the Terms and Conditions of his Resignation. Text: Your notice of immediate resignation received via email on 08 April 2024 at 09h37 is noted. 01:06:47 Govan: Won’t Gold for Life say that you’re just a disgruntled employee? 01:06:54 Mavuso: They can say whatever they want about me, but I have resigned. Why I’m hiding my identity? I don’t want people to be coming after me, because I put my face out there selling them this idea. V/O: The Mint of Norway has now requested a full audit of all the Mandela coins bought and sold. Text: The SA Gold Coin Exchange has assured us that a reputable external audit firm will conduct an independent audit. V/O: And hopefully they’re not paper coins. Because with the price of gold shooting through the roof, clients will be keen to cash in.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: A whistle blower has come forward to give details of how customers are scammed by Gold for Life. According to him "They are selling coins they don't have." They might have coins in their Scoin shops in various malls throughout the country, but these are purely for display purposes. Even if you pay cash for a coin, or set of coins, they will not hand it over straightaway. They have a mandatory 45 working days collection policy. After the 45 days has passed, that's when the real wait begins. They will come up with a multitude of excuses and hoops to jump through before you can collect your coins. Another scam is the safe custody option, SafeGold, where they offer to store your gold coins for a fee: 1 year - R1500; 3 year - R3500; 5 year - R5500; 10 years - R10 000. This includes insurance in the event that your coins are stolen. If you want to collect your coins you have to provide a POP to show you are paid up for this service. You also sign a contract with clear terms and conditions. However, our whistleblower claims there is NO safe custody. They simply sell your coins and when you notify them of your intention to collect, they will make you wait months, if not years before you get your coins.
metadata.Summary: Following on our previous story which showed how the Scoin shops "collectible" Mandela coins are not a worthwhile investment, we will show how Gold for Life (a subsidiary of Scoin and the SA Gold Exchange - all owned by Alan Demby & son Rael Demby) targets low income South Africans with the promise of a safe investment. However, their products are over-priced, and once the sale is concluded customers have to wait months of not years to receive their coins. What's more they are paying for safe storage of their coins, when in fact there is no vault or storage facility. This amounts to fraud.
metadata.Further information: The Scoin shop's Mandela coins are minted in Norway because the SA Mint refused to make them here. Most customers who pay a premium for these coins, are then offered less than half their value when they want to sell them. One case study has been notified that he can collect his coins on Friday 7 March from Head Office at The Marc. Gold for Life, Scoin and the SA Gold Exchange are NOT members of SAAND. SAAND (South African Association of Numismatic Dealers) is a respected organization with reputable and trustworthy members in the numismatic industry. Our members aim to promote fairness and transparency in the buying and selling of rare and collectible coins.
